title: Lecture 1: Introduction to the Course & History of ML
notes: Machine learning: algorithms that improve their performance at task T with experience E, measured by P.
The historical evolution from symbolic AI to statistical machine learning.
Taxonomy: Supervised learning, Unsupervised learning, and Reinforcement learning.

transcript.text: Hello and welcome to this course on Machine Learning. I am Balaraman Ravindran from IIT Madras.
Machine learning has become the defining paradigm for extracting actionable knowledge from large datasets.
Tom Mitchell's classic definition: a computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P.
We will explore how models generalize beyond observed training points to unseen test samples.

title: Lecture 2: Overview of Machine Learning Paradigms
notes: Supervised learning: regression (continuous outputs) and classification (categorical labels).
Unsupervised learning: clustering, dimensionality reduction, and density estimation.
The role of inductive bias in learning algorithms.

transcript.text: In this lecture we provide a high-level overview of the major learning paradigms.
In supervised learning, every training sample comes paired with an ground truth target value.
Without an inductive bias, every unobserved input is equally likely to have any label whatsoever.

module_title: Week 2: Linear Algebra for Machine Learning
title: Lecture 3: Why Linear Algebra? Scalars, Vectors & Matrices
notes: Why linear algebra forms the language of machine learning: data as high-dimensional feature vectors.
Vector addition, scalar multiplication, and geometric representation.
Matrix representations of multi-sample datasets.

transcript.text: Linear algebra is the foundational mathematical backbone of modern machine learning.
Each data instance is encoded as an n-dimensional vector residing in feature space R^n.
A dataset of m examples with n features naturally forms an m by n matrix X.

module_title: Week 2: Linear Algebra for Machine Learning
title: Lecture 4: Basic Operations in Linear Algebra
notes: Dot products of vectors and projection interpretation.
Matrix multiplication as linear transformations.
Transpose of a matrix and symmetric matrices.

transcript.text: Today we review fundamental algebraic operations: dot products, matrix products, and transpositions.
The inner product x^T y measures geometric similarity: ||x|| ||y|| cos(theta).
Matrix-vector product Ax corresponds to taking a linear combination of the column vectors of A.

module_title: Week 2: Linear Algebra for Machine Learning
title: Lecture 5: Vector Norms and Inner Products
concept_name: L1, L2 and Lp Vector Norms
notes: Definition of vector norm: non-negativity, triangle inequality, absolute homogeneity.
L2 Euclidean norm, L1 Manhattan norm, and L_infinity maximum norm.
Norms as regularization penalties (Ridge vs Lasso).

transcript.text: Norms measure the length or magnitude of vectors and appear constantly in loss functions.
The L2 norm is the standard Euclidean length, while the L1 norm sums absolute values.
We will see how L1 regularization encourages sparsity in feature selection.

title: Lecture 6: Linear Combinations, Span & Linear Independence
notes: Linear combinations of vectors: sum of alpha_i * v_i.
Span of a set of vectors as a subspace.
Linear independence: only trivial combination yields the zero vector.
Basis and dimensionality of vector spaces.

transcript.text: Lecture 6 explores span, linear independence, and basis vectors.
If a vector can be written as a combination of others, it provides no new independent dimension.
A minimal spanning set forms a basis, and its cardinality defines the dimension.

title: Lecture 7: Matrix Operations & Special Matrices
notes: Column space, row space, and null space of a matrix.
Matrix rank and full-rank matrices.
Orthogonal matrices: Q^T Q = I.
Positive semi-definite (PSD) matrices in covariance and kernel machines.

transcript.text: In this lecture we examine special matrix classes and the fundamental subspaces.
The rank of a matrix equals the dimension of its column space, which matches row rank.
Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and angles under linear transformations.

title: Lecture 8: Introduction to Probability Theory & Distributions
notes: Sample space, sigma-algebra, and Kolmogorov axioms of probability.
Random variables: discrete probability mass functions (PMF) and continuous density functions (PDF).
Cumulative distribution functions (CDF).

transcript.text: Week 4 begins our study of probability theory, the mathematical tool for reasoning under uncertainty.
A random variable maps outcomes in a sample space to real numbers.
For continuous random variables, probability of any single point is zero, but integrals over intervals are positive.

title: Lecture 9: Conditional, Joint & Marginal Probability
notes: Joint probability distribution P(X, Y) across multiple variables.
Marginalization: summing or integrating out nuisance variables.
Conditional probability P(X | Y) = P(X, Y) / P(Y).
Chain rule of probability.

transcript.text: In machine learning we frequently work with joint observations of features X and target Y.
The joint distribution contains all information about how X and Y co-occur.
Marginalization recovers P(X) by summing P(X, Y) over all possible values of Y.

title: Lecture 10: Bayes' Theorem & Inference Examples
notes: Bayes' Theorem: P(theta | D) = P(D | theta) * P(theta) / P(D).
Prior probability, likelihood, evidence, and posterior probability.
Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) vs Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE).

transcript.text: Bayes' Theorem is the fundamental engine for statistical updating in artificial intelligence.
The prior captures our beliefs before seeing data; the likelihood measures how well parameters explain the observations.
Multiplying prior and likelihood and normalizing produces the posterior distribution.

title: Lecture 11: Statistical Independence & Conditional Independence
notes: Statistical independence: P(X, Y) = P(X) * P(Y).
Conditional independence: P(X, Y | Z) = P(X | Z) * P(Y | Z).
The Naive Bayes assumption in text classification and spam filtering.

transcript.text: Today we dissect independence and conditional independence.
Two events are independent if knowledge of one tells us nothing about the other.
In Naive Bayes, features are assumed conditionally independent given the class label.

title: Lecture 12: Mathematical Expectation in ML
notes: Definition of mathematical expectation E[X] = sum(x * p(x)).
Linearity of expectation: E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y] regardless of independence.
Expected risk and empirical risk minimization (ERM).

transcript.text: Expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random quantity.
Linearity of expectation is an immensely useful property that holds even when variables are correlated.
Machine learning aims to minimize expected risk over the true data distribution.

title: Lecture 13: Variance, Covariance & Covariance Matrices
notes: Variance Var(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2] measures dispersion.
Covariance Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - mu_x)(Y - mu_y)].
Covariance matrix Sigma: positive semi-definite matrix of pairwise covariances.
Role of covariance in Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

transcript.text: In this lecture we define variance, covariance, and the covariance matrix Sigma.
Covariance indicates whether two variables tend to increase together or in opposite directions.
The eigenvectors of the empirical covariance matrix define the principal directions of variance.

title: Lecture 14: Relations for Expectation & Covariance
notes: Transformation of random variables and moments.
Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X).
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for random variables: |Cov(X, Y)| <= sqrt(Var(X) Var(Y)).

transcript.text: Lecture 14 formalizes algebraic identities for expectations and variances under linear transformations.
When we apply an affine transformation y = Ax + b, the new covariance matrix is A Sigma A^T.
Correlation coefficient rho bounds pairwise relationship strictly in [-1, +1].

title: Lecture 15: Machine Representation of Numbers & Floating Point
notes: IEEE 754 floating point standard: sign, exponent, mantissa.
Underflow, overflow, and numerical cancellation.
Log-sum-exp trick for stable probability computation in softmax and cross-entropy.

transcript.text: Computers do not work with real numbers; they work with finite-precision floating point representations.
Multiplying many small probabilities causes numerical underflow to zero.
By shifting by the maximum log-term, the log-sum-exp trick prevents underflow and overflow entirely.

title: Lecture 16: Derivatives, Gradient, Hessian & Jacobian
notes: Partial derivatives and the gradient vector grad(f) pointing in steepest ascent direction.
Jacobian matrix of vector-valued functions.
Hessian matrix of second derivatives and curvature / convexity tests.

transcript.text: Optimization in high dimensions relies on multivariable calculus: gradients, Jacobians, and Hessians.
The gradient vector grad f(x) contains all first partial derivatives.
The Hessian matrix describes local curvature. If the Hessian is positive definite everywhere, f is strictly convex.

title: Lecture 17: Matrix Calculus & Optimization Foundations
notes: Numerator vs denominator layout conventions.
Derivatives of linear forms: d/dx (a^T x) = a.
Derivatives of quadratic forms: d/dx (x^T A x) = (A + A^T) x.
Deriving ordinary least squares normal equations: (X^T X) w = X^T y.

transcript.text: Today we master matrix calculus notation to compute derivatives with respect to weight vectors.
Setting the gradient of the Mean Squared Error loss to zero directly yields the normal equations.
If X^T X is invertible, we get the analytical solution w = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y.

title: Lecture 18: Unconstrained Optimization & Gradient Descent
notes: Unconstrained optimization: minimizing f(w) over w in R^d.
Gradient descent update rule: w := w - alpha * grad(f(w)).
Learning rate alpha selection, oscillation, and divergence.
Convex vs non-convex optimization landscapes.

transcript.text: Gradient descent is the primary computational algorithm powering contemporary deep learning.
We take iterative steps in the direction opposite to the gradient vector.
For convex functions, gradient descent is guaranteed to converge to the global minimum with an appropriate step size.

title: Lecture 19: Introduction to Constrained Optimization & KKT
notes: Equality constraints and Lagrange multipliers.
Inequality constraints and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions.
Primal and dual optimization problems; weak and strong duality.
Application to maximum-margin hyperplanes in Support Vector Machines (SVM).

transcript.text: When optimization parameters must satisfy physical or regulatory constraints, we use Lagrange duality.
The KKT conditions generalize Lagrange multipliers to inequality constraints.
This dual formulation allows the kernel trick in Support Vector Machines.

title: Lecture 20: Introduction to Numerical Optimization Algorithms
notes: Batch Gradient Descent vs Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) vs Mini-batch SGD.
Momentum and acceleration methods for ravines and high-curvature surfaces.
Adaptive learning rate methods: AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam.

transcript.text: Lecture 20 concludes our foundational mathematics with practical stochastic optimization algorithms.
Evaluating gradients over millions of training samples is computationally prohibitive, so SGD samples minibatches.
Momentum accumulates past velocity vectors to accelerate traversal along consistent directions and damp oscillations.
